title: Ratio, Proportion, Partnership & Ages
summary: Ratio technique with its three biggest exam containers: proportion (mean/third/fourth proportional), partnership (capital × time profit splits) and ages (present vs shifted ratios). Tier 1 reliably has 2 questions from this cluster; most are 30–45 second marks once the multiplier habit is built.

subtopics.title: Ratio basics & dividing amounts
subtopics.concept:
A ratio $a : b$ compares two quantities of the same kind. Scaling both terms by the same number leaves it unchanged: $2:3 = 8:12$.

Write the quantities as $ax$ and $bx$. The multiplier $x$ turns every extra fact — sum, difference, product — into a small equation.

formulas.name: Combining ratios
formulas.tex: A:B = m:n,\ B:C = p:q \Rightarrow A:B:C = mp : np : nq

tricks.title: x solves everything
tricks.body: Translate 'ratio a : b' into ax and bx. Every extra fact becomes one small equation in x.

example.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 7 and their difference is 12. Find their sum.

tricks.title: LCM bridging for three terms
tricks.body: Scale A : B so its B-term matches the B-term of B : C, then read off A : B : C.

example.q: If A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, find A : B : C.

tricks.title: One share known, get the rest
tricks.body: Share = fraction × total. Recover the total from one share, then build any other share.

example.q: Rs 1,200 is divided between A and B in the ratio 2 : 3. Find B's share.

mistakes.wrong: Adding ratios term-wise: A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5 read as 2:3:5.
mistakes.right: Bridge the shared B: A:B:C = 8:12:15.

mistakes.wrong: Shifting a ratio by n years or n rupees.
mistakes.right: Shift the actual quantities (ax ± n), never the ratio terms.

mistakes.wrong: Comparing ratios by their differences (b − a).
mistakes.right: Cross-multiply: a:b beats c:d exactly when ad > bc.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing units inside one ratio.
mistakes.right: Convert first: 3 kg to 500 g is 3000 : 500 = 6 : 1.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'the ratio becomes p : q' as more information about the same x pair.
mistakes.right: It is the same x pair — write both statements with one x and equate.

subtopics.notes:
### One idea: the multiplier x
"Numbers are in ratio $a : b$" means the numbers are $ax$ and $bx$. The $x$ is one shared unit.

- Sum given: $(a+b)x = S$.
- Difference given: $(b-a)x = D$.
- Product given: $abx^2 = P$.

Two numbers in $5 : 7$ differ by 12: $2x = 12$, so $x = 6$ and the sum is $12x = 72$.

> **Rule:** Never argue with the ratio itself. Convert to $ax$, $bx$, and solve for x.

### Dividing an amount
Split N in $a : b : c$: one part $= \dfrac{N}{a+b+c}$, then multiply by each term.

Rs 780 in $3 : 4 : 6$: one part $= \dfrac{780}{13} = 60$, so the shares are 180, 240 and 360.

Questions often hide the total. "A gets Rs 300 more than B" gives $(b-a)x = 300$ — recover x, then the total is $(a+b+c)x$.

A difference works the same way. Rs 1,870 in $4 : 7$: eleven parts of 170, so the shares are 680 and 1,190 and Y gets $\dfrac{1870}{11} \times 3 = 510$ more than X. One division answers every share, every difference and the total.

> **Tip:** Compute the value of one part first; every share follows by multiplication.

### The LCM bridge
Given $A : B = 2 : 3$ and $B : C = 4 : 5$, make the two B-terms equal. The LCM of 3 and 4 is 12, so scale the first ratio by 4 and the second by 3: $A : B = 8 : 12$ and $B : C = 12 : 15$.

Read them together: $A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15$.

In symbols, $A:B = m:n$ and $B:C = p:q$ give $A:B:C = mp : np : nq$.

### The equality form
"$2A = 3B = 4C$" — take the LCM of 2, 3, 4, which is 12. Each letter equals $\dfrac{12}{\text{its multiplier}}$, so $A : B : C = 6 : 4 : 3$.

> **Watch:** Each term is LCM ÷ its own multiplier. A bigger multiplier means a smaller term.

### When the ratio changes
"Add k and the ratio becomes $p : q$": write $\dfrac{ax + k}{bx + k} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ and cross-multiply once.

Boys : girls $= 4 : 5$. After 100 boys join it is $6 : 5$. Now $\dfrac{4x + 100}{5x} = \dfrac{6}{5}$ gives $20x + 500 = 30x$, so $x = 50$ and the school had $9 \times 50 = 450$ students.

Both ratio statements describe the same x. That is the whole trick.

### Which ratio is larger
To compare $a : b$ with $c : d$, cross-multiply: $a : b$ is larger exactly when $ad > bc$.

$3 : 4$ or $5 : 7$? Compare $3 \times 7 = 21$ with $4 \times 5 = 20$. So $3 : 4$ is the larger ratio.

### Squares and roots of ratios
The **duplicate** ratio of $a : b$ is $a^2 : b^2$; the **sub-duplicate** is $\sqrt{a} : \sqrt{b}$. Squares with sides in $2 : 3$ have areas in $4 : 9$ — one squaring step.

> **Note:** Ratio terms must share one unit. 3 kg to 500 g is $3000 : 500 = 6 : 1$, never $3 : 500$.

subtopics.title: Proportion & proportional division of terms
subtopics.concept:
Four numbers $a, b, c, d$ are in proportion when $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}$. Cross-multiplying gives $ad = bc$: the outer pair multiplies to the same as the inner pair.

Three named proportionals: **fourth** $= \dfrac{bc}{a}$, **third** $= \dfrac{b^2}{a}$, **mean** $= \sqrt{ab}$.

Componendo and dividendo turns a sum-over-difference into a plain ratio: $\dfrac{x+y}{x-y} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ gives $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{p+q}{p-q}$.

tricks.title: Extremes times means
tricks.body: Set up the proportion in the exact order given, cross-multiply, done.

example.q: Find the fourth proportional to 4, 9 and 12.

tricks.title: Mean proportional = geometric mean
tricks.body: Multiply the two numbers and take the square root. Exam numbers make it a perfect square.

example.q: Find the mean proportional between 25 and 81.

tricks.title: Componendo-dividendo jump
tricks.body: When $(x + y)$ and $(x - y)$ both appear, jump straight to $x/y$ by adding and subtracting the given ratio's terms.

example.q: If $\dfrac{x+y}{x-y} = \dfrac{5}{3}$, find $\dfrac{x}{y}$.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping third and fourth proportional.
mistakes.right: Third repeats the middle term (b²/a); fourth uses three different terms (bc/a).

mistakes.wrong: Taking the arithmetic mean (a+b)/2 as the mean proportional.
mistakes.right: Mean proportional is the geometric mean √(ab).

mistakes.wrong: Reordering the terms before writing the proportion.
mistakes.right: Keep the question's order: 4, 9, 12 gives 27 but 12, 9, 4 gives 3.

mistakes.wrong: Using componendo-dividendo as (p+q)/(p−q) on the wrong side.
mistakes.right: Sum-over-difference equals p/q means x/y = (p+q)/(p−q); check which side is the sum.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the middle term repeats in a continued proportion.
mistakes.right: b appears in both fractions: a/b = b/c, so b² = ac.

subtopics.notes:
### What proportion means
$a : b :: c : d$ means $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}$, and cross-multiplication gives $ad = bc$.

$a$ and $d$ are the **extremes** (outer terms); $b$ and $c$ are the **means** (middle terms). Product of extremes = product of means. Every "find the missing term" question is one cross-multiplication away.

> **Rule:** $ad = bc$ for $a : b :: c : d$ — outer times outer equals middle times middle.

### The three named proportionals
- **Fourth proportional** to $a, b, c$: solve $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}$, so $d = \dfrac{bc}{a}$. Four different numbers.
- **Third proportional** to $a, b$: solve $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{b}{x}$, so $x = \dfrac{b^2}{a}$. The middle term repeats.
- **Mean proportional** between $a$ and $b$: $x = \sqrt{ab}$, from $\dfrac{a}{x} = \dfrac{x}{b}$.

Worked: fourth to 8, 12, 18 is $\dfrac{12 \times 18}{8} = 27$. Third to 9, 12 is $\dfrac{144}{9} = 16$. Mean between 12 and 48 is $\sqrt{576} = 24$.

> **Watch:** The mean proportional is the geometric mean $\sqrt{ab}$, never the average $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$. The average of 3 and 12 is 7.5, but the answer is 6.

### Continued proportion
$a, b, c$ are in continued proportion when $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{b}{c}$, that is $b^2 = ac$.

So the middle term is automatically the mean proportional of the outer two, and each member recovers from the others: $a = \dfrac{b^2}{c}$, $c = \dfrac{b^2}{a}$, $b = \sqrt{ac}$.

Three numbers $x, 12, 18$ in continued proportion: $144 = 18x$, so $x = 8$. Check $\dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{12}{18} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

### A worked chain
"Three numbers $a, b, c$ are in continued proportion, $b = 12$ and $a + c = 26$."

Then $ac = 144$, and $a, c$ are the factor pair of 144 that sums to 26: 8 and 18. The numbers are 8, 12, 18.

Exam numbers are built so the factor pair is clean. If yours is not, re-read the question, not the method.

### Componendo and dividendo
If $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}$, then $\dfrac{a+b}{a-b} = \dfrac{c+d}{c-d}$.

The exam use runs it backwards: given $\dfrac{x+y}{x-y} = \dfrac{p}{q}$, jump to $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{p+q}{p-q}$.

$\dfrac{x+y}{x-y} = \dfrac{5}{3}$ gives $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$. No solving — one addition and one subtraction.

> **Tip:** A sum-over-difference equal to a ratio is the fingerprint. Componendo-dividendo is the intended route.

### Coefficient twists
$\dfrac{5x - 3y}{5x + 3y} = \dfrac{2}{7}$. Apply the rule to get $\dfrac{5x}{3y} = \dfrac{7+2}{7-2} = \dfrac{9}{5}$, then rearrange: $25x = 27y$.

Write the two fractions with plus on top and minus below before adding and subtracting. Sign slips are the only failure here.

### Order matters
Fourth proportional to 4, 9, 12 is 27, but fourth proportional to 12, 9, 4 is 3. The terms stay in the order written — copy the proportion exactly as the question lists it.

Sanity check: x² = ab; the average (a+b)/2 is the planted trap.

subtopics.title: Partnership
subtopics.concept:
Profit is divided in the ratio of **capital × time** — the capital-months.

Same period for all partners: time cancels, so the share ratio is just the capital ratio. Different joining dates or mid-year top-ups: build one capital-months row per partner.

A working partner's fee or per cent comes off the profit **first**; only the residue is divided.

tricks.title: One row per partner
tricks.body: Write capital × months for each partner; the profit ratio is the row ratio.

example.q: A invests Rs 12,000 for the full year; B joins after 4 months with Rs 18,000. Divide a Rs 9,600 profit.

tricks.title: Cut comes off the top
tricks.body: Salary or a per cent for the manager is removed from the whole profit before the capital-months split.

example.q: A and B invest Rs 6,000 and Rs 4,000. B manages and takes 10% of a Rs 9,000 profit. Find A's share.

tricks.title: Equal shares, find the capital
tricks.body: Equal shares mean equal capital-months. Equate the products and solve.

example.q: A invests Rs 12,000 for 12 months. B joins after 6 months and they share the profit equally. Find B's capital.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring time when partners join on different dates.
mistakes.right: Share ∝ capital × months; compute capital-months for everyone.

mistakes.wrong: Counting a late joiner's months from the year's start.
mistakes.right: Months run from the joining month to the year end.

mistakes.wrong: Sharing the profit first and taking the manager's cut after.
mistakes.right: The cut comes off the top; only the residue is split.

mistakes.wrong: Using only the final capital after a mid-year change.
mistakes.right: Add capital × months across each stretch of the year.

mistakes.wrong: Answering the working partner's split share when the total receipt is asked.
mistakes.right: Add the cut back to that partner's share when 'in all' is asked.

subtopics.notes:
### One rule for everything
Profit share $\propto$ capital $\times$ time. Call the product **capital-months**.

Same period for everyone: the time cancels, and the share ratio is just the capital ratio. Different joining dates, withdrawals or top-ups: build one row per partner and add up.

> **Rule:** Share $\propto$ capital $\times$ months. Nothing else matters in this topic.

### The capital-months table
A invests Rs 12,000 for 12 months. B joins after 4 months with Rs 18,000, so B's money works only 8 months.

| Partner | Capital-months |
|---|---|
| A | $12000 \times 12 = 144000$ |
| B | $18000 \times 8 = 144000$ |

Ratio 1 : 1 — a Rs 9,600 profit splits 4,800 each. A late joiner can catch up only by investing more.

> **Tip:** A late joiner's months run from the joining month to the year end, never from the start.

### Mid-year capital changes
Split the year at each change and add capital × months.

A invests 15,000 for 4 months and 20,000 for 8: $60000 + 160000 = 220000$. Against B's $18000 \times 12 = 216000$, the ratio is $55 : 54$.

Same engine for withdrawals: A holds 30,000 for 8 months then 20,000 for 4, giving $240000 + 80000 = 320000$ capital-months.

> **Watch:** Using only the first capital or only the final capital is the classic error on these.

### The working partner's cut
A partner who manages the business takes a fee or a per cent of the profit **off the top**. Only the residue is divided by capital-months, and the working partner's own capital still counts in that split.

Profit 9,000; B manages and draws 10%: cut 900, residue 8,100 split by capitals $3 : 2$. B's split share is 3,240, and B's total receipt is 4,140 if the question asks for it.

> **Careful:** The cut applies to the whole profit, not to the residue. And take it off before sharing, not after.

### Rent of a pasture
The same engine in rural costume: animals are the capital, months are the months.

A grazes 15 cows for 8 months (120 cow-months); B grazes 25 cows for 4 months (100). Rent 2,200 splits $6 : 5$, so A pays 1,200 and B pays 1,000.

### Wages and workmen
Wages for a job split the same way: men × days. Three men working 5, 8 and 10 days share wages in $5 : 8 : 10$. Nothing new to learn — capital-months again.

Rs 1,200 split for 2, 3 and 5 days worked: ten parts of 120, so the shares are 240, 360 and 600.

### Keep the numbers small
Drop zeroes early: 12,000 × 12 is 144 thousand-months. Ratios survive any common division, and every zero you drop is one less slip. When the products look unwieldy, divide all of them by 1,000 before forming the ratio.

patterns.howToSpot: 'A invests X and adds or withdraws Y after k months' — one partner's capital moves mid-year.
steps: Split the year at every change.
Add capital × months over the stretches.

patterns.name: Working partner (cut off the top)
patterns.howToSpot: 'A manages the business and gets x% of the profit' — or a fixed salary — before the rest is shared.
steps: Take the working partner's cut out of the profit first.
Divide the residue by the capital ratio (the working partner's capital still counts).
Add the cut back if that partner's total receipt is asked.
patterns.why: The fee pays for work done, so it must not pass through the profit ratio.

patterns.howToSpot: Grazing rent divided among farmers whose herds graze for different periods.
steps: Count cow-months for each farmer: animals × months.
The rent ratio is the ratio of these products.
Multiply each share of the ratio by the total rent.
patterns.why: The pasture is the partnership: animals are the capital, months are the months.

Same time for all: pure capital ratio.
Late joiner: months from joining to year end.
Mid-year change: add capital-months per stretch.
Working partner: cut off the top, split the residue.
Pasture rent and wages: the same capital-months engine.

subtopics.title: Problems on ages
subtopics.concept:
Three facts never change: each age grows by 1 every year, the sum of two ages grows by 2 per year, and the **difference** between two ages is constant forever.

Standard template: present ages in ratio $a : b$, a second ratio $n$ years later (or earlier). Write $ax$, $bx$ and solve $\dfrac{ax \pm n}{bx \pm n} = \dfrac{p}{q}$.

One multiplier is always enough.

formulas.name: Constant difference
formulas.tex: A - B \text{ is the same at every time}

formulas.name: Multiple of age
formulas.tex: F = kS \Rightarrow F \pm n = k'(S \pm n)
formulas.note: k falls over time for elder-younger pairs.

tricks.title: Multiplier plus shift
tricks.body: Ages $ax$, $bx$ now; shift both by n; equate the new ratio; solve for x.

example.q: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. After 8 years the ratio becomes 3 : 4. Find the sum of their present ages.

tricks.title: Use the constant difference
tricks.body: The gap between two ages never changes — compute it once and reuse it at any time point.

example.q: A father is 3 times as old as his son. Eight years ago he was 5 times as old. Find their present ages.

tricks.title: Bracket the present with two ratios
tricks.body: With 'n years ago' and 'n years hence' ratios, both snapshots share one x — the 2n shift separates them.

example.q: Six years ago A : B was 5 : 6, and six years hence it will be 6 : 7. Find B's present age.

mistakes.wrong: Shifting the ratio terms: 5 : 7 after 8 years read as 13 : 15.
mistakes.right: Shift the ages: (5x + 8) and (7x + 8).

mistakes.wrong: Adding n to only one person's age.
mistakes.right: Every living person's age moves by n; the sum of two ages moves by 2n.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the ratio gap (b − a)x as the age gap at a shifted time.
mistakes.right: The age gap (b − a)x is fixed for all time — that is exactly why it is useful.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the multiple rise over time for elder-younger pairs.
mistakes.right: The multiple falls: 4 times now, 3 times later, closer to 1 eventually.

mistakes.wrong: Solving the two-snapshot system with n instead of 2n.
mistakes.right: From 'n years ago' to 'n years hence' each age moves 2n years.

subtopics.notes:
### The three facts that never change
- Each person's age grows by 1 every year. Shift n years: add n to both ages.
- A sum of two ages grows by 2n over n years.
- The difference between two ages never changes. A 32-year gap now is a 32-year gap forever.

> **Rule:** Shift the ages, never the ratio. $5 : 7$ today is not $5+n : 7+n$ tomorrow.

### The multiplier template
Present ages in ratio $a : b$ — write $ax$ and $bx$. A shifted ratio becomes one equation:

$$\frac{ax + n}{bx + n} = \frac{p}{q} \quad (\text{after } n \text{ years}), \qquad \frac{ax - n}{bx - n} = \frac{p}{q} \quad (n \text{ years ago})$$

One cross-multiplication gives x. $5 : 7$ now and $3 : 4$ after 8 years: $\dfrac{5x+8}{7x+8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$ gives $20x + 32 = 21x + 24$, so $x = 8$. Ages 40 and 56, sum 96.

If the question gives a sum or difference of present ages instead, $(a+b)x$ or $(b-a)x$ is that value — no shift needed.

### Sum and difference shortcuts
Ratio $3 : 4$ with sum 35: seven parts of 5, so 15 and 20. The younger is 15.

The sum grows by 2 a year: "the sum is 40 now; what was it 5 years ago?" — 30, no ratio needed. Read which year the question means before dividing by parts.

### k-times questions
"Father is k times the son" — write father $= k \times$ son, with the son as the single unknown.

Mother 4 times the daughter; after 5 years, 3 times: $4d + 5 = 3(d + 5)$, so $d = 10$ and the mother is 40. The gap of 30 never moved: 45 and 15 give exactly 3 times.

> **Watch:** For an older-younger pair the multiple falls over time — 4 times becomes 3 times. If your answer grows the multiple, flip the equation.

### Two shifted ratios
A ratio n years ago AND n years hence give two equations in the same x.

Ten years ago $2 : 3$; ten years hence $4 : 5$. Present ages are $2x + 10$ and $3x + 10$. The second snapshot: $\dfrac{2x + 20}{3x + 20} = \dfrac{4}{5}$ gives $10x + 100 = 12x + 80$, so $x = 10$ and A is 30.

The 2n years between the two snapshots is the easiest slip: each age changes by 2n, not n.

### The constant-difference check
After solving, verify the gap is the same at both times. Father 48, son 16: gap 32. Eight years ago, 40 and 8 — gap 32, ratio 5, matching "5 times as old".

The check also runs forwards. A man is 25 years older than his son and will be exactly twice his age in ten years. Then $s + 35 = 2(s + 10)$, so the son is 15 now. In ten years the pair is 25 and 50 — gap still 25.

> **Tip:** Compute the age gap once and reuse it at every time point. It kills wrong options without solving.

### Three people
Ratios among three people work the same: $4x, 5x, 6x$. Exams add one pairwise fact ("A is 6 years older than C" gives $2x = 6$) because more would over-determine the problem.

subtopics.title: Money ratios: income–expenditure, coins & mixed amounts
subtopics.concept:
Two classic money containers for ratios.

**Income and expenditure:** incomes in $a : b$, expenditures in $p : q$. Write incomes $ax, bx$ and expenditures $py, qy$ — two multipliers — then use each person's savings.

**Coin bags:** price one full set of coins in the ratio; divide the total value by the set value; multiply back for any count.

formulas.name: Savings equations
formulas.tex: ax - py = s_1,\quad bx - qy = s_2
formulas.note: Two multipliers: x for incomes, y for expenditures.

tricks.title: Subtract the savings equations
tricks.body: Write both savings equations and subtract — equal savings kill the constant and one variable.

example.q: Incomes of A and B are in the ratio 8 : 5 and expenditures in 5 : 3. If each saves Rs 1,200, find A's income.

tricks.title: Value per set for coins
tricks.body: Take one full set of coins in the given ratio, price it in paise, and scale.

example.q: A bag has 50-paise, 25-paise and 10-paise coins in the ratio 7 : 6 : 5 amounting to Rs 550. Find the number of 25-paise coins.

tricks.body: For 'A gets half of B, B gets two-thirds of C', give the last-named person the unit and read the ratio off.

mistakes.wrong: Using one multiplier for both income and expenditure ratios.
mistakes.right: Incomes take x, expenditures take y — two letters, two equations.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing paise and rupees in coin problems.
mistakes.right: Convert everything to one unit first; Rs 1 = 100 paise.

mistakes.wrong: Answering the value of the coins when the count is asked (or the reverse).
mistakes.right: Read whether the question wants a count or a value; both sit in the options.

mistakes.wrong: Comparing days instead of rates when workers work together.
mistakes.right: Together, shares follow 1/days.

mistakes.wrong: Accepting a negative expenditure multiplier.
mistakes.right: A negative y means the equations were set up with swapped multipliers.

subtopics.notes:
### Two ratios, two multipliers
Incomes in $a : b$ and expenditures in $p : q$. Write incomes $= ax$, $bx$ and expenditures $= py$, $qy$.

Two different multipliers — mixing them is the standard error. Savings give one equation per person: $ax - py = s_1$ and $bx - qy = s_2$.

> **Rule:** Incomes take x, expenditures take y. Never one letter for both.

### Equal savings — subtract
Each saves Rs 2,000 with incomes $9 : 7$ and expenditures $4 : 3$:

$$9x - 4y = 2000, \qquad 7x - 3y = 2000$$

Subtract: $2x = y$. Then $9x - 8x = 2000$, so $x = 2000$ and A's income is 18,000.

Another: incomes $8 : 5$, expenditures $5 : 3$, each saves 1,200. Subtracting gives $3x = 2y$, so $y = 1.5x$. Then $8x - 7.5x = 0.5x = 1200$, so $x = 2400$ and A's income is 19,200.

Equal savings cancel on subtraction — that is what makes these questions short.

### Unequal savings — eliminate
When the savings differ, scale one equation so y matches, then subtract. Same two-line shape, one extra multiplication.

### A complete walkthrough
Incomes $5 : 4$, expenditures $3 : 2$, each saves Rs 1,600. So $5x - 3y = 1600$ and $4x - 2y = 1600$.

Equal savings, so subtract: $x - y = 0$, meaning $x = y$. Then $5x - 3x = 2x = 1600$, so $x = 800$.

Incomes 4,000 and 3,200; expenditures 2,400 and 1,600. Both savings check out at 1,600.

### Coin bags
Coins in ratio $n_1 : n_2 : n_3$ of denominations $d_1, d_2, d_3$. Price ONE set: $n_1d_1 + n_2d_2 + n_3d_3$. Then sets = total value ÷ set value, and a coin's count = its term × sets.

Rs 1, 50-paise and 25-paise coins in $5 : 8 : 4$ worth Rs 210: a set is $500 + 400 + 100 = 1000$ paise $=$ Rs 10. So 21 sets, and the 50-paise coins number $8 \times 21 = 168$.

> **Careful:** Convert everything to paise (or everything to rupees) before pricing the set. Rs 1 = 100 paise.

The same engine counts total coins: Rs 5, Rs 2 and Rs 1 coins in $3 : 5 : 7$ worth Rs 512. A set is Rs 32, so 16 sets, and the total coins are $15 \times 16 = 240$.

### Wages in proportion to work
Wages follow work done. Days worked: shares $\propto$ days. Working together: shares $\propto$ work rates, $\dfrac{1}{\text{days}}$.

Workers finishing alone in 6 and 9 days earn in ratio $\dfrac{1}{6} : \dfrac{1}{9} = 3 : 2$. Of Rs 1,500, the faster worker gets 900.

> **Watch:** Together, compare $\dfrac{1}{\text{days}}$, never the days themselves.

### Chained fractions
"A $= \dfrac{3}{4}$ of B and B $= \dfrac{4}{5}$ of C" gives $A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 5$. Build the three-term ratio on a common base before touching any money.

### Statement-defined shares
"A gets half of B; B gets two-thirds of C." Let the third hold 3: then B $=$ 2 and A $=$ 1. Ratio $1 : 2 : 3$; Rs 918 gives A $= \dfrac{918}{6} = 153$.

> **Tip:** Take the last-named person as the base unit; every statement becomes a whole-number multiple.

solvedExamples.q: A sum of ₹2,500 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. What is the largest share?
If A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 3, then A : B : C is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Make the B-parts equal: LCM of 4 and 2 = 4.
A : B = 3 : 4 stays; B : C = 2 : 3 becomes 4 : 6.
So A : B : C = **3 : 4 : 6**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: B = 4: scale the second ratio by 2. Answer 3 : 4 : 6 (option 6 : 8 : 9 is the trap from wrong scaling).

solvedExamples.q: Find the third proportional to 12 and 18.
A and B enter into a partnership. A invests ₹30,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹40,000 for 6 months. At the end of the year they earn a profit of ₹28,800. Find A's share.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Profit ratio is capital × time = 3 : 2 ⇒ A gets 3/5 of ₹28,800 = ₹17,280.

solvedExamples.q: The present ages of two persons are in the ratio 4 : 5. After 16 years, the ratio of their ages will be 6 : 7. What is the sum of their present ages?
solvedExamples.solution:
Let present ages be $4x$ and $5x$.
$\frac{4x + 16}{5x + 16} = \frac{6}{7}$ ⇒ $28x + 112 = 30x + 96$ ⇒ $2x = 16$ ⇒ $x = 8$.
Present ages 32 and 40 ⇒ sum **72 years**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Cross-multiply once: 7(4x+16) = 6(5x+16) ⇒ x = 8 ⇒ sum = 9x = 72. (Constant difference 8 years never changes — good check.)

practice.solution:
Let the son be s; father = 3s.

Father = 3 × 16 = **48 years**.

Incomes 8x, 5x; expenditures 5y, 3y.
8x − 5y = 1200 and 5x − 3y = 1200.
Subtracting: 3x − 2y = 0 ⇒ y = 1.5x. Then 5x − 4.5x = 1200 ⇒ x = 2400.
A's income = $8 \times 2400$ = ₹19,200.
practice.shortcut: Two equations, subtract to kill one variable: y = 1.5x ⇒ 0.5x = 1200 ⇒ A = 8x = ₹19,200.

practice.solution:
B's management salary = 10% of 9,000 = ₹900. Residue = ₹8,100.
Capital ratio = 6,000 : 4,000 = 3 : 2.
A gets $\frac{3}{5} \times 8100$ = ₹4,860 (B gets ₹3,240 + ₹900 = ₹4,140).
practice.shortcut: Cut 10% off the top, split 3 : 2: A = 3/5 × 8,100 = ₹4,860.

$\frac{5x + 12}{6x + 12} = \frac{6}{7}$ ⇒ $35x + 84 = 36x + 72$ ⇒ $x = 12$.

₹1,200 is divided among three workers in proportion to the number of days each worked: 2 days, 3 days and 5 days. The share of the third worker is:
Working alone, two workers can finish a job in 6 days and 9 days respectively. They work together and receive ₹1,500 for the job. The first worker's share is:
practice.solution:
Shares follow work rate: $\frac{1}{6} : \frac{1}{9} = 3 : 2$.
First worker $= \frac{3}{5} \times 1500 = ₹900$.

A sum of ₹918 is divided among three friends such that the first gets half of what the second gets, and the second gets two-thirds of what the third gets. The first friend's share is:
practice.solution:
Take the third = 3 → second $= \frac{2}{3} \times 3 = 2$ → first $= 1$.
Ratio $1 : 2 : 3$ → first $= \frac{1}{6} \times 918 = ₹153$.
